There is no disagreement among people that the meaning is "with knowledge from Us that they were people of choosing," so the clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl).

He, glorified is He, mentioned their being chosen and the wisdom in His choosing them, and He mentioned His knowledge, which indicates the places of His wisdom and His choosing.

(Benefit)

The context guides one toward clarifying what is general, specifying what is ambiguous, establishing with certainty that the unintended meaning is not possible, restricting what is generic, qualifying what is absolute, and recognizing the variety of implication.

This is among the greatest indicators revealing the intended meaning of the speaker. Whoever neglects it errs in his understanding and argues fallaciously in his debate.

Consider the words of the Most High: ﴿Taste! Indeed, you were the mighty, the noble﴾. How you find its context indicates that he is the abased, the contemptible.

He says: 'O Lord, give him.' Then he is crowned with kings and clothed with a garment of honour. Then He says: 'Are you pleased?' He says: 'O Lord, I desire for him better than this.' So Allah gives him the kingdom in his right hand and eternity in his left. Then He says to him: 'Are you pleased?' He says: 'Yes, O Lord.'"

Imam Ahmad mentioned in the Musnad, from the hadith of Abu Burdah, from his father, raising it [to the Prophet (ﷺ)]:

"Learn Surat al-Baqarah, for taking it is a blessing and leaving it is regret, and the *Batalah* (sorcerers) cannot master it." Then he was silent for a while, then said: "Learn Surat al-Baqarah and Al 'Imran, for they are the two Zahrawan (the two luminous ones), and they will shade their companion on the Day of Resurrection like two clouds, or two canopies, or two flocks of birds in ranks. The Qur'an will say: 'I am the one who made you thirsty in the midday heat and kept your night awake, and every merchant is behind his trade, and you today are behind every trade.' Then he is given the kingdom in his right hand and eternity in his left, and a crown of dignity is placed upon his head, and his two parents are clothed with two ornaments the world cannot equal. He said: 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Khaythamah related to us: al-Hasan ibn Musa related to us: Ibn Lahi'ah related to us: Daraj Abu al-Samh related to me that Abu al-Haytham related to him, from Abu Sa'id, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that a man said to him: "O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), blessed (*tuba*) is the one who saw you and believed in you." He said: "Blessed is the one who saw me and believed in me, and blessed, then blessed, is the one who believed in me and did not see me." A man said to him: "And what is *Tuba*?" He said: "A tree in Paradise, the distance of a hundred years. The garments of the people of Paradise come out of its sheaths."

He said: Ya'qub ibn 'Ubayd related to me: Yazid ibn Harun related to us: Hammad ibn Salamah informed us, from Abu al-Muhazzam, who said: Abu Hurayrah said:

"The dwelling of the believer in Paradise is a pearl, in which is a tree that grows garments. A man takes with his two fingers (and he pointed with the index and thumb) seventy garments, embroidered with pearls and coral."

He said: Hamzah ibn al-'Abbas related to us: 'Abd Allah ibn 'Uthman related to us: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us: Safwan ibn Hamzah informed us, from Shurayh ibn 'Ubayd, who said: Ka'b said:

"If a garment of the garments of the people of Paradise were worn today in this world, whoever looked at it would faint, and their eyes could not bear it."

'Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak said: Sulayman ibn al-Mughirah informed us, from Humayd ibn Hilal, from Bishr ibn Ka'b or someone else, who said:

"It was mentioned to us that the wife among the wives of Paradise has seventy garments, which are finer than this your [piece of] thin cloth (*shaqiq*), and the marrow of her shin can be seen from behind the flesh."

In the two Sahihs also, from the hadith of al-Bara', who said: A silk garment was given as a gift to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they began to marvel at its softness. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "You marvel at this? The handkerchiefs of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh in Paradise are better than this."

There is no hiding what there is in the specific mention of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh here, for he was among the Ansar in the position of al-Siddiq among the Muhajirun. The Throne shook at his death. He never feared the blame of any blamer in [the cause of] Allah. Allah concluded his life with martyrdom, preferred the pleasure of Allah and His Messenger over the pleasure of his people, his clan and his allies, and his judgment agreed with the judgment of Allah above the seven heavens. Gabriel announced his death to the Prophet (ﷺ) on the day he died. So it is fitting that the handkerchiefs with which he wipes his hands in Paradise are better than the garments of kings.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on Surah 44, verses 51–53:**

*Al-maqam* is the place of dwelling. *Al-amin* is that which is safe from every evil, blight and harm.

[The Paradise described] is the one that has gathered all the qualities of safety. It is safe from cessation, ruin and every kind of deficiency. Its people are safe within it from departure, deficiency and distress. A secure town is one whose people are safe within it from what they would fear from others.

Reflect on how Allah, glorified is He, mentioned safety in His words: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in a secure place﴾

And in His words, exalted is He: ﴿There they call for every kind of fruit, in security﴾

So He combined for them the safety of the place and the safety of the food. They do not fear the fruit being cut off, nor its bad consequences or harm, nor the prospect of leaving it. They do not fear any of this. And [they are safe from] death, so they fear no death there.

**(Benefit)**

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in a secure place, among gardens and springs. They will wear fine silk and brocade, facing one another. Thus [it will be], and We will marry them to fair ones with wide, lovely eyes. There they call for every kind of fruit, in security. They will not taste death therein except the first death. And He will protect them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire﴾.

He combined for them the goodness of the abode, the attainment of safety in it from every harm, its containing fruits and rivers, the goodness of clothing, the perfection of companionship through facing one another, the completeness of pleasure through the wide-eyed companions (*al-hur al-'in*), their calling for all kinds of fruit, together with their safety from its cessation, its harm and its danger. And the conclusion of all this is that He informed them that they will not taste death there.

**(Section: on the clothing, ornaments, cushions, couches, beds and rugs of the people of Paradise)**

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in a secure place, among gardens and springs, wearing fine silk and brocade, facing one another﴾

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds—indeed, We do not waste the reward of one who does good work. For those will be gardens of perpetual residence, beneath which rivers flow. They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold, and they will wear green garments of fine silk and brocade, reclining therein on couches﴾

Another group said: the intended meaning is not the thick one, but the dense one (*al-saftq*).

Al-Zajjaj said: they are two kinds of silk. The most beautiful of colours is green, and the softest of garments is silk. So He combined for them the goodness of the appearance of the garment, the delight of the eye in it, and its softness, and the delight of the body in it.

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And their clothing therein is silk﴾.

"Indeed, Allah, mighty and majestic, has an angel since the day He created [the world], who fashions the ornaments of the people of Paradise until the Hour rises. If a single piece of the ornaments of the people of Paradise were brought out, it would outshine the light of the sun's rays. So do not ask after this about the ornaments of the people of Paradise."

Al-Hasan ibn Yahya ibn Kathir al-'Anbari related to us: my father related to us, from Ash'ath, from al-Hasan, who said:

"The ornaments in Paradise are more beautiful on men than on women."

Al-Hasan ibn Yahya ibn Kathir al-'Anbari related to us: my father related to us, from Ash'ath, from al-Hasan, who said:

"The ornaments in Paradise are more beautiful on men than on women."

"If a man of the people of Paradise appeared and showed his bracelet, it would obliterate the light of the sun, just as the sun obliterates the light of the stars."

"They are adorned with gold and silver, encrusted with pearls, and upon them are crowns of pearls and rubies, interlinked, and upon them is a crown like the crowns of kings. They are youths, beardless, with kohl in their eyes."

It is related in the two Sahihs, and the wording is Muslim's, from Abu Hazim, who said: I was behind Abu Hurayrah while he was performing ablution for prayer, and he would extend his hand until it reached his armpit. I said: "O Abu Hurayrah, what is this ablution?" He said: "O my nephew of the clan of Farrukh, were you here? If I had known that you were here, I would not have performed this ablution. I heard my beloved (*khalili*) say: 'The ornament will reach the believer to the extent that the ablution reaches.'" And whoever holds that washing the upper arm and prolonging it is recommended has taken evidence from this.

In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said:

"Whoever enters Paradise will be in bliss and will not be miserable; his garments will not wear out, and his youth will not decay. In Paradise there is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived."

As for his words, "his garments will not wear out," the apparent meaning is that the specific garments will not be subject to wear. It is also possible that the intended meaning is the kind, rather, that new garments are always upon him, just as the eating of food does not cease within its kind, but every food is succeeded by another. And Allah knows best.

Imam Ahmad said: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi related to us: Muhammad ibn Abi al-Wada' related to us: al-'Ala' ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Rafi' related to us: Hunan ibn Kharijah related to us, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, who said: A Bedouin from the Haram came and said: "O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), tell us about the emigration (*hijrah*) to you: wherever you are, or for a specific people, or to a known land? If I die, [does it end]?" He asked three times, then sat down. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) remained silent for a little while, then said: "Where is the questioner?" He said: "Here he is, O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." He said: "Emigration is to abandon indecencies, what is apparent of them and what is hidden, to establish prayer and give zakat. Then you are a muhajir, even if you die in your homeland." Then another man stood and said: "O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), tell me about the garments of the people of Paradise: are they created or woven?" He said: some of the people laughed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do you laugh at an ignorant man who asks a learned one?" The Prophet (ﷺ) was silent for a while, then said: "Where is the questioner about the garments of the people of Paradise?" He said: "Here he is, O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." He said: "No, rather, they are split from the fruit of Paradise," three times.

Al-Tabarani said in his Mu'jam: Ahmad ibn Yahya al-Hulwani and al-Hasan ibn 'Ali al-Fasawi related to us, both saying: Sa'id ibn Sulayman related to us: Fudayl ibn Marzuq related to us, from Abu Ishaq, from 'Amr ibn Maymun, from 'Abd Allah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said:

"The first group to enter Paradise will have faces like the light of the moon on the night of the full moon. The second group will be upon the colour of the brightest star in the sky. This chain meets the condition of the Sahih.

Imam Ahmad said: Yunus ibn Muhammad related to us: al-Khazraji related to us, from 'Uthman al-Sa'di: Abu Ayyub, the freedman of 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, related to us, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

He said: I said: "O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), what is the *nasif*?" He said: "The *khimar*."

Ibn Wahb said: 'Amr informed us that Daraj Abu al-Samh related to him, from Abu al-Haytham, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

"A man will recline in Paradise for seventy years before he shifts. Then a woman will come to him and strike him on his shoulders, and he will look at his face in her cheek, which is clearer than a mirror. Indeed, the smallest pearl upon her would illuminate what is between East and West. She greets him, he returns the greeting, and he asks her, 'Who are you?' She says, 'I am al-Mazid (the One of Increase).' Al-Tirmidhi related the mention of the crowns and "the smallest pearl" from Suwayd ibn Nasr, from Rushdin ibn Sa'd, from 'Amr, with this [wording].

Ibn Abi al-Dunya said: Muhammad ibn Idris al-Hanzali related to us: Abu 'Utbah related to us: Isma'il ibn 'Ayyash related to us, from Sa'id ibn Yusuf, from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir, from Abu Sallam al-Aswad, who said: I heard Abu Umamah relate from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said:

In the two Sahihs also, from the hadith of al-Bara', who said: A silk garment was given as a gift to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they began to marvel at its softness. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "You marvel at this? The handkerchiefs of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh in Paradise are better than this."

"Wa-l-hur" is the plural of "hawra'" (ḥawrāʾ). It refers to a young, beautiful, fair woman, with the whiteness of the eye intensely white and the blackness of the eye intensely black.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: the ḥawrāʾ is she in whom the gaze is dazzled. "ʿIn" means women with beautiful eyes. Mujahid said: the ḥawrāʾ is she in whom the gaze is dazzled, owing to the delicacy of the skin and the purity of the complexion.

Al-Hasan said: the ḥawrāʾ is one in whom the whiteness of the eye is intense and the blackness of the eye is intense.

The derivation of this word has been disputed. Ibn ʿAbbas said: in the speech of the Arabs, "al-ḥawr" means whiteness.

Likewise Qatadah said: "al-ḥawr" means the white ones.

Muqatil said: "al-ḥawr" means those with white faces. Mujahid said: "al-ḥur al-ʿin" are those in whom the gaze is dazzled, whose leg-marrow shows through their garments, and the beholder sees his face in the liver of one of them, like a mirror, owing to the delicacy of the skin and the purity of the complexion. This is an agreed point.

The word is not derived from bewilderment (ḥayrah). The root of ḥawr is whiteness, and taḥwīr is whitening. The sound view is that ḥawr is derived from ḥawr in the eye (ḥawr al-ʿayn), which is the intense whiteness of the eye together with the strength of its blackness. Thus it includes both meanings.

In the Ṣiḥāḥ of al-Jawhari, "al-ḥawr" is the intense whiteness of the eye along with the intensity of its blackness, and a woman is ḥawrāʾ when the ḥawr is clearly evident.

Abu ʿAmr said: ḥawr means that the whole eye is black, like the eyes of gazelles and cows. There is no ḥawr among the children of Adam; the women were only called "ḥūr al-ʿayn" because they were likened to gazelles and cows.

Al-Asmaʿi said: "I do not know what ḥawr in the eye is."

I say: Abu ʿAmr differed from the lexicographers regarding the derivation of the word, returning ḥawr to blackness, whereas others returned it to whiteness, and to whiteness within blackness.

Ḥawr in the eye is a meaning that combines the goodness of whiteness and blackness and their harmony, each gaining beauty from the other.

It is said "ʿayn ḥawrāʾ" when the whiteness of its white part and the blackness of its black part are intense.

A woman is not called ḥawrāʾ unless, together with the ḥawr of her eyes, there is whiteness of body complexion.

"Al-ʿin" is the plural of ʿaynāʾ, which is a woman with large eyes. A man is "aʿyan" if he has large eyes. A woman is "ʿaynāʾ," and the plural is "ʿin." The sound view is that "al-ʿin" are those women whose eyes have gathered the qualities of beauty and grace.

Muqatil said: "al-ʿin" means women with beautiful eyes. Among the beauties of a woman is the breadth of her eye in length; narrowness of the eye in a woman is a defect.

﴿And We wed them to ḥūr ʿīn﴾

Abu ʿUbaydah said: We made them into pairs, as a shoe is paired with a shoe. We made them two by two.

Yunus said: We joined them with them, and this is not the sense of a marriage contract. He said: The Arabs do not say "tazawwajtu bihā" (I married with her); they say "tazawwajtuhā."

Ibn Nassr said: This, and the revelation, supports what Yunus said.

This is God's saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when Zayd had accomplished his need from her, We wed her to you﴾

Had it been "tazawwajtu bihā," it would have said "zawwajnāka bihā."

Ibn Salam said: The Tamim say "tazawwajtu imraʾah" and "tazawwajtu bihā." Al-Kisa'i also related this.

Al-Azhari said: The Arabs say "zawwajtuhu imraʾah" and "tazawwajtu imraʾah," and it is not in their speech to say "tazawwajtu bi-imraʾah."

(Benefit)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We wed them to ḥūr ʿīn﴾

That is, We joined them with them.

Al-Farra' said: This is a dialect of the Azd Shanuʾah.

Al-Wahidi said: Abu ʿUbaydah's view on this is better, because he made it from "tazwīj" in the sense of making a thing into a pair, not in the sense of concluding a marriage contract.

From this it is permissible to say: "He was single, so I paired him with another," as one says "I split it with another."

The preposition "bi" is prohibited by those who prohibit it only when the meaning is the concluding of a marriage contract.

I say: It is not impossible that both meanings are intended together. The word "tazwīj" indicates marriage, as Mujahid said: "We married them to the ḥūr." The particle "bi" indicates conjunction and union, and this is more eloquent than omitting it. And God knows best.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 44, verse 56:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They shall not taste therein death, except the first death﴾

This is from the exception whose time is the time of the excepted-from (al-istithna' al-sabiq zamanuhu zaman al-mustathna minhu). Since the first death is of the same kind as the death that has been negated, some have claimed that it is a connected exception (muttasil).

Some others said: "illa" (except) here means "ba'da" (after).

The meaning would be: they shall not taste death in Paradise after the first death.

This is a very good meaning, but it requires the wording to support it. What clarifies this is that the intention is not to exclude the first death from the negated death, nor is there any supposed thing which would require an exception for it. Rather, the intention is to inform that after their first death, which Allah decreed for them, they will not taste any other.

On this basis it is said: since the ruling after illa is different from the ruling before it, and everlasting life in Paradise only comes after the first death, the particle "illa" conveyed this meaning of "afterness." Confusion is avoided because the first death is not included in the negated death in Paradise, so the particle was stripped down to this meaning.

This is among the best things said about the verse, so reflect upon it.

And he said in (al-Madarij):

As for His saying: ﴿They shall not taste therein death, except the first death﴾

This exception is for affirming the continuance of life and the absence of tasting death. It makes the first, general negation like a text to which no exception whatsoever can apply, for if an exception of one of its individual instances were admissible, it would have been more fitting to mention it than to turn away to the disconnected exception (al-istithna' al-munqati'). So this exception functions as emphasis and as an explicit safeguarding of the generality. This applies to every disconnected exception, so reflect upon it, for it is among the secrets of the Arabic language.
